outcome: As of 12 Oct 2026 no source establishes f(n) = 2^(n-2)+1 for any n >= 7, so the problem is open for every n >= 7 (exact values are known only for n <= 6). Since 26 Jan 2024 the events bearing on it are: a partial SAT attack on n = 7 covering only certain anchored families of 33-point sets (Bogdan, arXiv 30 Dec 2025, preprint, still described as open); a split-polygon relaxation and a proof of the conjecture for decomposable point sets only (Baek and Balko, SoCG 2025, 20 Jun 2025); a 2026 journal record reporting a weak-k-gon variant bound (C_weak(7) > 33) that I could not read directly; and neighbouring variants (empty hexagons, lines, higher dimensions, above-below functions, a benchmark listing) that do not change the planar statement.
problem_asks: Statement (Wikipedia Jan 2024): 'Solving the happy ending problem for arbitrary n'. Let f(n) be the least N such that any N points in the plane, no three on a line, contain n points in convex position. The statement asks for f(n) for every n >= 3, i.e. (a) the exact value of f(n) for each n >= 3. Read through the Erdos-Szekeres conjecture, this is (b) proving f(n) = 2^(n-2)+1 for all n >= 3, which splits into (b1) the lower bound 2^(n-2)+1 <= f(n), which is classical (1960 construction) and holds for all n, and (b2) the upper bound f(n) <= 2^(n-2)+1, which is what is open. (c) The values for n = 3, 4, 5, 6 are already known (f(3)=3, f(4)=5, f(5)=9, f(6)=17), so the open content of 'arbitrary n' is n >= 7. Nothing in the frozen bullet asks only for an asymptotic or a bound: 'solving for arbitrary n' is read here as determining f(n) for every n, which is what the bullet's wording asks for. An asymptotic result answers a different question.

events.what_happened: Erdos and Szekeres posed the problem and proved f(n) <= C(2n-4, n-2)+1 in Compositio Mathematica 2 (1935) 463-470 (as cited by the Wikipedia article and by erdosproblems.com #107). Background only; it predates the window.
events.delivers: Upper bound f(n) <= C(2n-4, n-2)+1 for every n, of exponential order 4^n. Poses the problem.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: the exact value of f(n) for every n >= 3 and the matching upper bound 2^(n-2)+1.

events.what_happened: Erdos and Szekeres gave explicit constructions proving f(n) >= 2^(n-2)+1 for all n >= 3 and conjectured equality. Cited as 1960 on erdosproblems.com #107 and as 1961 ('On some extremum problems in elementary geometry', Ann. Univ. Sci. Budapest) on Wikipedia. Background only; it predates the window.
events.delivers: Lower bound f(n) >= 2^(n-2)+1 for every n >= 3, with explicit point sets of size 2^(n-2) containing no n points in convex position. The conjecture is that these are extremal.
events.remains: The matching upper bound f(n) <= 2^(n-2)+1 for every n >= 7 (for n <= 6 see the small-case events).
events.directly_checkable: Yes: the constructions are explicit point sets. Wikipedia illustrates a 16-point set with no convex hexagon; the construction was not re-checked by us.
events.direction: Lower-bound direction. The explicit sets are the extremal examples the conjecture predicts, so they do not contradict it.
events.object: Explicit family of 2^(n-2) points in general position with no n points in convex position (Erdos-Szekeres construction). Non-constructive existence is not involved.

events.what_happened: Small cases. f(4)=5 is credited to Klein (1931 per erdosproblems.com #107; 1932 per a search summary, so the year conflicts). f(5)=9 is attributed to Makai and Turan with no year on erdosproblems.com; the first published proof is Kalbfleisch, Kalbfleisch and Stanton, 'A combinatorial problem on convex regions', Proc. Louisiana Conf. (1970), per Wikipedia. Background only; it predates the window.
events.delivers: f(4)=5 and f(5)=9 exactly.
events.remains: Every n >= 6, in particular n >= 7 for the problem.
events.direction: Confirms the conjectured formula for n = 4, 5.

events.what_happened: Szekeres and Peters, 'Computer solution to the 17-point Erdos-Szekeres problem', ANZIAM J. 48 (2006) 151-164: an exhaustive computer enumeration establishing f(6)=17 (every 17-point set in general position contains a convex hexagon; 16 points can avoid one). Per Wikipedia and erdosproblems.com, this is the last n for which the value is known. Predates the window.
events.delivers: f(6)=17 exactly, by computer enumeration (not a human-readable argument).
events.remains: Every n >= 7.

machine_checked.system: Exhaustive computer enumeration (not formal); later formalised in Isabelle/HOL by Maric (see the 2017 event)

events.what_happened: Balko and Valtr, 'A SAT attack on the Erdos-Szekeres conjecture': SAT solving (Glucose) refutes the Peters-Szekeres conjecture (a stronger 2006 conjecture about two-colourings of the ordered complete 3-uniform hypergraph). Per their page the work also uses Erdos-Tuza-Valtr techniques to refine the planar conjecture for SAT solvers. The page reports an extended abstract in Electronic Notes in Discrete Mathematics 49 (2015) 425-431, last updated 28 Nov 2016; the European J. Combin. 66 (2017) 13-23 publication is from a search summary. Predates the window.
events.revisions: Extended abstract 2015; page last updated 28 Nov 2016; full paper in EJC 66 (2017) per a search summary

events.remains: The planar statement f(n) = 2^(n-2)+1 for all n >= 7.
events.direction: Cuts against the hypergraph variant of the conjecture (a stronger analogue). It does not touch the planar statement.
events.object: A 2-colouring of the complete ordered 3-uniform hypergraph on 33 vertices with no monochromatic 7-gon, per the page's file list. The planar meaning of that object is not stated on the page.

events.what_happened: Andrew Suk, 'On the Erdos-Szekeres convex polygon problem', arXiv:1604.08657 (v1 29 Apr 2016, v2 27 Aug 2016). Abstract: 'we nearly settle the Erdos-Szekeres conjecture by showing that ES(n) = 2^(n+o(n))'. Explicit bound ES(n) <= 2^(n+6n^(2/3) log n) for large n. Quanta (30 May 2017) and Wikipedia cite JAMS 2017; the journal page was not opened. Predates the window.
events.delivers: ES(n) = 2^(n+o(n)): the exponential rate, for all large n. Does not determine the exact value 2^(n-2)+1.
events.remains: The exact value of f(n) for every n >= 7 (the o(n) term leaves the constant in the exponent open).

events.what_happened: Filip Maric, 'Fast formal proof of the Erdos-Szekeres conjecture for convex polygons with at most 6 points', J. Automated Reasoning (DOI 10.1007/s10817-017-9423-7). Date 2017 is the online year; the issue year is given as 2019 by another record. Independently, Scheucher and Maric verified g(6)=17 by SAT (per Heule and Scheucher). Predates the window.

events.what_happened: Jineon Baek (University of Michigan) and Martin Balko (Charles University), 'The Erdos-Szekeres Conjecture Revisited', SoCG 2025, LIPIcs vol. 332, article 13, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.SoCG.2025.13; published 20 June 2025 per the Ben-Gurion repository record. Results: (i) every planar set of at least 2^(k-2)+1 points, no three collinear, contains a 'split k-gon' (Theorem 3), and the threshold is tight; (ii) the conjecture is proved for 'decomposable' point sets (Theorem 8; the statement with a = u = k confirms the conjecture for decomposable sets); (iii) an ordered 3-uniform hypergraph generalisation is false; (iv) new constructions of 2^(k-2) points with no k points in convex position, generalising all previously known ones. The full text also says 'Our SAT-solver-based proofs show that this is also the case for weak k-gons.' The earliest public version has not been established (see incomplete).
events.revisions: None found in the sources read. A journal version is listed separately (2026 event).
events.delivers: For the split-k-gon relaxation: threshold 2^(k-2)+1, tight. For the convex-position problem: the conjecture holds for decomposable point sets only, a restricted class. For general planar point sets: nothing.
events.remains: f(n) = 2^(n-2)+1 for every n >= 7 for arbitrary planar point sets, and the general statement for every n >= 3 beyond the decomposable class. The paper's own abstract calls the general conjecture still open.

events.what_happened: Dumitru Bogdan (Faculty of Computer Science, University of Bucharest; arXiv lists 'Bogdan Dumitru'), 'Notes on the 33-point Erdos-Szekeres problem', arXiv:2512.24061 (v1 30 Dec 2025, the only version listed). Attacks the first open planar case, ES(7) = 33. SAT encoding with triple-orientation variables, a 4-set convexity criterion that excludes convex 7-gons, and convex-layer anchoring constraints; solved single-threaded with Kissat via PySAT. Reports only UNSAT outcomes: UNSAT certificates for several anchored families (templates in Table 1; single-thread times from about 2.5e3 s to 2.28e6 s; base instance 578,336 variables and 16,670,808 clauses before hull constraints). States that the k = 7 case 'remains open' and that the planar 33-point question is not decided.
events.delivers: Within the anchored families in Table 1 (described only by templates in the paper), no 33-point configuration avoids a convex 7-gon, i.e. f(7) <= 33 for those families. Nothing for general 33-point sets. No lower-bound construction and no counterexample.
events.remains: f(7) = 33 for all 33-point sets, and f(n) for every n >= 8.

disputes.summary: The bound f(n) <= 2^(n+O(sqrt(n log n))) for planar points is attributed to Holmsen, Mojarrad, Pach and Tardos by erdosproblems.com #107 and by Wikipedia. The arXiv abstract for arXiv:1710.11415 (as fetched) states the same form for c(n) and c'(n), which are functions on convex bodies, and attributes the planar point bound to Suk. A search summary also gives the error term as O(k log k). Which paper states the planar-point form was not settled from the paper text.
Author name order for Bogdan's paper differs: arXiv lists 'Bogdan Dumitru', and the PDF header gives 'Dumitru Bogdan'. Likely the same person; not treated as a dispute.

The year of the Erdos-Szekeres lower bound paper is 1960 on erdosproblems.com and 1961 on Wikipedia. The year of the first f(4)=5 result is 1931 on erdosproblems.com and 1932 in a search summary. Dates are recorded as given, with the conflicts visible.

summary: Found: no source establishes f(n) = 2^(n-2)+1 for any n >= 7, and erdosproblems.com #107 (last edited 11 Apr 2026, accessed 12 Oct 2026) still presents the problem as open, with its edit history showing only typographical changes since 20 Oct 2025. The planar-point events in the window are two. First, Baek and Balko (SoCG 2025, LIPIcs, 20 Jun 2025) prove a tight threshold for split k-gons, confirm the conjecture for decomposable point sets, show a hypergraph generalisation false, and give new 2^(k-2)-point constructions; the general planar conjecture remains open. This is a restricted-class result, and whether it counts as a case of the problem is for the judging pass. Second, Bogdan (arXiv:2512.24061, 30 Dec 2025) gives UNSAT certificates for SAT encodings of anchored families of 33-point sets, implying f(7) <= 33 for those families only; the paper says the k=7 case remains open. The strongest case for the Bogdan result is that it is genuine progress on the n=7 case; the strongest case against it is that it covers only anchored families and is unreviewed beyond its single arXiv version. The journal record in JCTA (vol. 222, 2026) reports C_weak(7) > 33 for a weak-k-gon variant, per a search summary I could not verify against the paper; the SoCG text read via a summarising fetch already contains the sentence 'Our SAT-solver-based proofs show that this is also the case for weak k-gons', so that claim may date from June 2025. Neighbouring work does not change the planar statement: empty-hexagon h(6)=30 (Heule and Scheucher, Mar 2024; Lean follow-up Mar 2024), lines (Furukawa, Sep 2024), higher dimensions (Scheucher 2021; Pohoata and Zakharov 2022), a 2026 weighted monotone-subsequence namesake (Erdos 1026), a 2026 Koshelev-Koshka SAT/ASP paper on coloured variants, and the 2026 Chen-Pohoata above-below paper on R^d functions. The FrontierMath Erdos benchmark (6 Sep 2026) lists #107 as an open benchmark item, with no solution claimed. AI involvement: no AI system is credited with any mathematics on the planar problem in any source I read. Searches of the AI-results lists (the Gemini Aletheia paper with its 13 problems, the AlphaProof Nexus paper with 9 solved problems, the GitHub AI-contributions wiki) show no row for #107. The only AI credits found are on neighbouring problems: Aristotle on the namesake #1026, and ChatGPT on the 2026 above-below upper bound, the latter from an acknowledgements excerpt I could not confirm in the full PDF. Other AI-adjacent items seen but off-problem: the OpenAI unit-distance disproof (May 2026) and reports of Claude Mythos on the same unit-distance problem; neither is about convex position. The Epoch benchmark page's remark that Bloom estimates 3 to 5 Erdos problems of this calibre had been solved by AI is secondary context only. Name note: the Moonlight review of Bogdan's paper is AI-generated commentary, recorded as checked_by with automated true, and is not evidence about how the paper was written.
competing_reading: A reader could count Baek and Balko's decomposable-sets theorem and Bogdan's anchored-family UNSAT certificates as cases of the problem under the 'case settled' reading of section 2 (a restricted class, or n=7 for certain families). On the strict scope reading, neither touches the statement for arbitrary planar point sets. Similarly, the JCTA weak-k-gon result could be read as evidence about the planar conjecture if the weak variant is treated as a stronger analogue, but the summary suggests it refutes only the weak analogue. The Holmsen et al. bound is either the best known upper bound for planar points (per erdosproblems.com and Wikipedia) or a bound on convex bodies (per the arXiv abstract as fetched), and the judging pass should pick the reading the paper supports.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The JCTA article text (DOI 10.1016/j.jcta.2026.106195): the definition of weak k-gon, the C_weak(7) > 33 proof, and whether it is the same paper as the SoCG version. (2) The full text of Bogdan's arXiv paper: the anchored families, the transfer argument on omitted 5-point clauses, and any published certificate or code. (3) An earlier public version of the Baek-Balko split-polygon and decomposable-set results, to date them (a talk file with metadata dated 15 Jan 2024 was not readable). (4) The Chen-Pohoata PDF acknowledgements, to confirm or retract the ChatGPT sentence. (5) The FrontierMath Erdos scoring table, to see whether any system has attempted problem 107. (6) A change in the erdosproblems.com #107 status or a new citing paper that resolves a case.

incomplete: (1) The JCTA paper (vol. 222, article 106195) could not be read: ScienceDirect returned 403 and the DOI redirect gave no content. The C_weak(7) > 33 claim, the Kissat 3.0.0 detail, and the 'weak k-gons' statement come from search summaries and are recorded as unverified. Whether this is the same paper as the SoCG 2025 version is unknown. (2) The Baek-Balko SoCG full text was read through a summarising fetch of the LIPIcs HTML, not directly; the PDF was binary. The earliest public version is not established: a Balko talk PDF whose file metadata is dated 15 Jan 2024 was unreadable, so the first public written argument may predate 26 Jan 2024 and predates_frozen_revision is left null. (3) Chen-Pohoata (arXiv:2605.27061): the PDF is binary and the acknowledgements were not read in full. The ChatGPT credit is taken from a search excerpt. The PDF was saved outside the project directory, and I did not read it there. (4) The Bogdan record rests on the arXiv HTML read through a summarising fetch; no artifact or certificate was found, and no independent check was located. (5) The Epoch FrontierMath page shows no per-problem results, so whether any model has attempted or solved #107 is unknown beyond the benchmark listing. (6) The Gemini (2601.22401) and AlphaProof Nexus (2605.22763) lists were checked only in part (see dead_ends). (7) The Holmsen et al. planar-point bound attribution is unresolved (see disputes). (8) Suk's JAMS publication, the Marić Isabelle paper's sorry-status and its volume/year, the Pohoata-Zakharov Duke publication, and the Scheucher CGT publication are all from search summaries or journal metadata, not from the journal pages. (9) The 1935 and 1960 Erdos-Szekeres papers and the Morris-Soltan survey were not opened; their details come from Wikipedia and erdosproblems.com. (10) The Heule-Scheucher full paper was read only at abstract level, so its certificate size and checking are not recorded. (11) The erdosproblems.com #216 page was seen only in a search summary. (12) The DeepMind Lean file's commit date is not shown, so the event date is the copyright year 2025.
